profile.feeling: Summer, salads and sauces — the base of countless Arab dishes.

senses.def: tomatoes, tomato (collective mass noun; one tomato = حَبَّةُ طَمَاطِمَ)

examples.tr: I love tomato salad.
I bought a kilo of tomatoes.
Add the tomato paste to the pot.
Tomato juice is good for you.

collocations.tr: one tomato (lit. a piece of tomatoes)

synonyms.nuance: the Levantine word, borrowed from Italian pomodoro; feminine, used in writing there too

etymology.text: Borrowed from Spanish tomate, from Classical Nahuatl tomatl, reshaped as a plural pattern (Wiktionary).

funFacts: One American fruit, two European routes: طَمَاطِم from Spanish tomate, بَنَدُورَة from Italian pomodoro.
pitfalls: Diptote: it looks like a broken plural (pattern faʿāʿil), so it never takes tanwīn and its genitive ends in -a: كِيلُو طَمَاطِمَ, not *طَمَاطِمٍ.
No standard unit noun: one tomato is حَبَّةُ طَمَاطِمَ.
subtleties: Wiktionary gives it as masculine (a collective); in recipes you will also see feminine adjectives, as if it were a plural: طَمَاطِمُ مُقَطَّعَةٌ (chopped tomatoes).

profile.feeling: Strong smell, kitchen tears.

examples.tr: Add the chopped onion to the oil.
The smell of onion is strong.
Cutting the onions made me cry.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym in Modern Standard Arabic.

etymology.text: Common Semitic word: akin to Hebrew בָּצָל (batsal), Phoenician bṣl, Aramaic būṣlā and Old South Arabian bṣl.

funFacts: Arabic بَصَل and Hebrew בָּצָל are the same Semitic word — learn them together.
pitfalls: Collective: الْبَصَلُ = onions (as food); one onion = بَصَلَة; counted onions = بَصَلَات.
subtleties: As a collective it takes masculine singular agreement: الْبَصَلُ رَخِيصٌ الْيَوْمَ (onions are cheap today).

profile.feeling: Comfort food: fries, stews, mashed potatoes.

senses.def: potatoes, potato (collective mass noun; one potato = حَبَّةُ بَطَاطِسَ)

examples.tr: I love French fries (fried potatoes).
I bought a kilo of potatoes.
Peel the potatoes and cut them up.

synonyms.nuance: the usual form in the Levant and North Africa — but in Egypt بَطَاطَا is the sweet potato

etymology.text: From Ottoman Turkish پاتاتس (patates), from Greek πατάτες (patátes), from Spanish patata, from Taíno batata (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The final -s is the Greek plural ending of πατάτες, which reached Arabic through Ottoman Turkish patates.
pitfalls: In Egypt بَطَاطَا means sweet potato: ask for بَطَاطِس for ordinary potatoes.
Diptote: no tanwīn, genitive in -a — كِيلُو بَطَاطِسَ.
subtleties: Wiktionary gives it as masculine or feminine; adjectives are usually feminine, as with a plural: بَطَاطِسُ مَقْلِيَّةٌ.

profile.feeling: Pungent, healthy, essential in Levantine and Egyptian cooking.

examples.tr: I don’t like the smell of garlic.
Add two cloves of garlic.
Garlic is good for the heart.
I bought a big bulb of garlic.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym in Modern Standard Arabic.

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ṯūm- (Wiktionary); cognate with Hebrew שׁוּם (shum).

funFacts: Hebrew שׁוּם (shum) is the same word: Arabic ث regularly matches Hebrew שׁ, as in ثَلَاثَة / שָׁלוֹשׁ (three).
pitfalls: ثُومَة is a whole bulb (head) of garlic; a single clove is فَصُّ ثُومٍ.
Sun letter: الثُّومُ is pronounced aṯ-ṯūm — the l of al- is not heard.
subtleties: Collective: الثُّومُ = garlic as food, with masculine singular agreement (الثُّومُ مُفِيدٌ).

profile.feeling: Fresh, summery.

examples.tr: Cucumber salad with yogurt is delicious.
I bought a kilo of cucumbers.
Peel the cucumber and slice it.

synonyms.nuance: classical (Qurʾānic) word for cucumber-like gourds; not the everyday cucumber today

etymology.text: Borrowed from Classical Persian خیار (xiyār).

funFacts: Turkish hıyar (cucumber) is the same Persian word.
pitfalls: خِيَار also means “choice, option” — same spelling, same vowels: لَيْسَ لَدَيَّ خِيَارٌ = I have no choice.
subtleties: One cucumber is خِيَارَة; the collective خِيَار is cucumbers as food.

profile.feeling: Levantine and Mediterranean home cooking.

examples.tr: We cook eggplant with meat.
I bought three eggplants.
Stuffed eggplant is a famous dish.

profile.synonymsNone: No common synonym in Modern Standard Arabic.

etymology.text: Borrowed from Classical Persian بَاذِنْگَان (bāzingān), ultimately from Sanskrit वातिङ्गण (vātiṅgaṇa).

funFacts: Through Arabic al-bāḏinjān came Spanish berenjena, Catalan albergínia and French — and German — aubergine.
pitfalls: Written with ذ (ḏ, as in English “this”), not ز: بَاذِنْجَان.
subtleties: Counting: ثَلَاثُ بَاذِنْجَانَاتٍ — numbers 3–10 take the opposite gender of the singular (بَاذِنْجَانَة is feminine, so ثَلَاث has no ة).

profile.feeling: Healthy, everyday food.

examples.tr: I love carrot juice.
I bought a kilo of carrots at the market.
My mother cut up a small carrot.

phrases.tr: the policy of the stick and the carrot

profile.synonymsNone: No everyday synonym in Modern Standard Arabic.

etymology.text: From Persian گزر (gazar).

funFacts: Hebrew גֶּזֶר (gezer) comes from the same Persian word.
pitfalls: جَزْر (jazr, with sukūn) is the ebb of the sea — الْمَدُّ وَالْجَزْرُ, high and low tide. Without vowel marks both are written جزر.
Collective: الْجَزَرُ = carrots (as food); one carrot = جَزَرَة; counted carrots = جَزَرَات.
subtleties: A collective takes masculine singular agreement: الْجَزَرُ مُفِيدٌ (carrots are healthy).

profile.feeling: Sweet, orange, autumn and winter food; roasted on the street in Egypt.

senses.def: sweet potato (lit. “sweet potato”, a noun + adjective phrase)

examples.tr: Sweet potatoes are rich in vitamins.
I bought sweet potatoes at the market.
We roast the sweet potatoes in the oven.

synonyms.nuance: on its own, the everyday word for sweet potato in Egypt (elsewhere it means the ordinary potato)

etymology.text: بَطَاطَا is borrowed from Spanish batata (Wiktionary); حُلْوَة is the feminine of حُلْو, “sweet”. Wiktionary’s translation tables give بَطَاطَا حُلْوَة for the sweet potato.

funFacts: English “potato” itself comes from batata, the Taíno name of the sweet potato, via Spanish.
pitfalls: In the Levant بَطَاطَا alone is the ordinary potato, in Egypt it is the sweet potato — in MSA add حُلْوَة to be clear.
subtleties: بَطَاطَا is indeclinable (it ends in -ā): only the adjective shows case and definiteness — بَطَاطَا حُلْوَةٌ / الْبَطَاطَا الْحُلْوَةَ. The adjective is feminine because بَطَاطَا is feminine.

profile.feeling: Home cooking: peas with meat and rice.

senses.def: peas (mass noun; one pea = حَبَّةُ بَازِلَّاءٍ)

examples.tr: My mother cooked peas with meat.
Add the peas and the carrots to the rice.
We bought frozen peas.

etymology.text: Borrowed from Italian piselli (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Greek μπιζέλι also comes from the Italian word for peas — a Greek speaker already half-knows بَازِلَّاء.
pitfalls: Double l (šadda) and a final hamza: بَازِلَّاء (bāzillāʾ). Spellings without the hamza are informal.
subtleties: A feminine mass noun (Wiktionary): بَازِلَّاءُ مُجَمَّدَةٌ (frozen peas). Wiktionary declines it as a triptote: بَازِلَّاءً، بَازِلَّاءٍ.

profile.feeling: Green, iron-rich, Levantine spinach pies.

senses.def: spinach (mass noun; one leaf = وَرَقَةُ سَبَانِخَ)

examples.tr: Spinach has a lot of iron.
I cook spinach with rice.
I bought a bunch of spinach.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym in everyday MSA; Wiktionary lists older alternative spellings such as إِسْفَانَاخ.

etymology.text: From Middle Persian; see Persian اسفناج (esfanâj) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The same Persian word became Turkish ıspanak, Greek σπανάκι and — through Arabic and Medieval Latin — English spinach.
pitfalls: Declined here as a diptote like طَمَاطِم (حُزْمَةُ سَبَانِخَ); Wiktionary also records triptote use (سَبَانِخٌ، سَبَانِخٍ) and the vowel variant سَبَانَخ.
Sun letter: السَّبَانِخُ = as-sabāniḫ.
subtleties: A mass noun: there is no unit noun; count leaves (وَرَقَةُ سَبَانِخَ) or bunches (حُزْمَةُ سَبَانِخَ).

profile.feeling: Crunchy and sharp; a side to salads and falafel plates.

examples.tr: I like radishes with salad.
I bought a bunch of radishes.
This radish tastes hot.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym in Modern Standard Arabic.

etymology.text: From Aramaic פּוּגְלָא (puḡlā, “radish”), from Akkadian puglu (“radish”); a wanderwort (Wiktionary).

funFacts: One of the oldest vegetable names in this course: it goes back through Aramaic to Akkadian puglu.
pitfalls: Also vocalized فِجْل (fijl); Wiktionary lists both. Besides the counted plural فُجْلَات, Wiktionary gives a broken plural فُجُول.
subtleties: Collective: الْفُجْلُ = radishes in general; one radish = فُجْلَة.

profile.feeling: Sweet autumn dishes.

examples.tr: My grandmother made a sweet from pumpkin.
Pumpkin is rich in vitamins.
We bought a big pumpkin.

synonyms.nuance: classical word for a gourd plant (Qurʾān 37:146, the plant over Jonah); also used for pumpkin
“honey pumpkin” — the sweet orange pumpkin, especially in Egypt

etymology.text: From Classical Syriac qarrʾā (Wiktionary).

funFacts: With u, قُرْعَة (qurʿa) is “a draw, a lottery” — from the root q-r-ʿ of casting lots; with a, قَرْعَة is one pumpkin.
pitfalls: قَرْع also means “knocking” (verbal noun of قَرَعَ, to knock): قَرْعُ الْبَابِ = knocking on the door.
subtleties: Collective الْقَرْع (pumpkin as food) vs. unit قَرْعَة (one pumpkin).

profile.feeling: Crisp, light, salads.

examples.tr: Lettuce salad is light.
Wash the lettuce well.
I bought a big head of lettuce.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym in Modern Standard Arabic.

etymology.text: From Aramaic חַסָּא (ḥassā), from Akkadian ḫassū (“lettuce”), from Sumerian; cognate with Hebrew חַסָּה (ḥassa) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew חַסָּה is the same word; both go back through Aramaic and Akkadian to Sumerian — lettuce has kept its name for over four thousand years.
pitfalls: خَسَّة is one head of lettuce — unvocalized it looks like خِسَّة, “meanness, baseness”.
The s is doubled (šadda): خَسّ = ḫass.
subtleties: Collective with masculine singular agreement: الْخَسُّ طَازَجٌ (the lettuce is fresh).

ref.src: Wiktionary (kaikki.org): فلفل; the phrase has no entry

profile.feeling: Heat and spice; loved in Yemen, Tunisia and Egypt, avoided by others.

examples.tr: I don’t eat hot chili peppers.

examples.text: أَضِفْ قَلِيلًا مِنَ الْفِلْفِلِ الْحَارِّ إِلَى الصَّلْصَةِ.
examples.tr: Add a little chili to the sauce.

examples.text: زَرَعَ جَدِّي فِلْفِلًا حَارًّا فِي الْحَدِيقَةِ.
examples.tr: My grandfather grew chili peppers in the garden.

synonyms.nuance: chili pepper, and also hot sauce or ground chili (Wiktionary); very common in Egypt

etymology.text: فِلْفِل is borrowed from Classical Persian پلپل (pilpil), from Sanskrit पिप्पलि (pippalī, “long pepper”) (Wiktionary); حَارّ means “hot”.

funFacts: Greek πιπέρι, English pepper and Arabic فِلْفِل all go back to Sanskrit pippalī.
pitfalls: Plain فِلْفِل is ambiguous — black pepper, sweet pepper or chili, depending on region and context. Add حَارّ for chili.
Also pronounced فُلْفُل (fulful).
subtleties: حَارّ also means “hot” in temperature: يَوْمٌ حَارٌّ (a hot day).

profile.feeling: Winter vegetable; stuffed cabbage rolls are a family dish.

senses.def: cabbage (mass noun; one head = رَأْسُ مَلْفُوفٍ)

examples.tr: We cook stuffed cabbage on Fridays.
I bought a head of cabbage.
Cabbage salad is delicious.

synonyms.nuance: the classical dictionary word, and the everyday word in Egypt and the Hijaz (Wiktionary); from Greek κράμβη

etymology.text: Derived from the passive participle of لَفَّ (laffa, “to wrap”) — literally “the wrapped (rolled-up) one” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: كُرُنْب comes from Greek κράμβη, and قَرْنَبِيط (cauliflower) from its diminutive κραμβίδιον — the cabbage family speaks Greek in Arabic.
pitfalls: مَلْفُوف is also the ordinary adjective “wrapped, rolled”: وَرَقُ عِنَبٍ مَلْفُوفٌ = rolled vine leaves. Context decides.
subtleties: In the Levant, Iraq and the Gulf you say مَلْفُوف; in Egypt and in older dictionaries you meet كُرُنْب (Wiktionary’s translation tables). Both are correct MSA.

profile.feeling: Fried cauliflower with tahini — a popular home dish.

senses.def: cauliflower (mass noun; one head = رَأْسُ قَرْنَبِيطٍ)

examples.tr: Fried cauliflower is a popular dish.
I bought a head of cauliflower.
Cut the cauliflower into small pieces.

synonyms.nuance: lit. “flower” — the everyday word for cauliflower

etymology.text: From Ancient Greek κραμβίδιον (krambídion), the diminutive of κράμβη (krámbē, cabbage); a doublet of كُرُنْب (Wiktionary).

funFacts: A Greek word for “little cabbage” became the Arabic word for cauliflower.
pitfalls: Egyptians pronounce it ʔarnabīṭ (q → glottal stop) but write قَرْنَبِيط.
subtleties: Masculine mass noun: الْقَرْنَبِيطُ الْمَقْلِيُّ (fried cauliflower).

profile.feeling: Modern, healthy, a newcomer to Arab markets.

senses.def: broccoli (mass noun, indeclinable; one head = رَأْسُ بْرُوكُلِي)

examples.tr: Broccoli is rich in vitamins.
I steam the broccoli.
I bought a head of broccoli.

profile.synonymsNone: No native word: the Italian loan is used everywhere.

etymology.text: Borrowed from Italian broccoli. Wiktionary has no Arabic entry; its translation tables vocalize the word بْرُوكُلِي or بْرُكُولِي, masculine.

funFacts: Italian broccoli is a plural: “little sprouts”, from brocco, “shoot”.
pitfalls: The spelling is not fixed: بروكلي, بروكولي and بركولي all occur, and the vowels vary. The initial cluster br- is kept, so the vocalized form starts with a sukūn: بْرُوكُلِي.
Indeclinable (ends in -ī): no case endings, only الـ for “the”.
subtleties: Masculine (Wiktionary): الْبْرُوكُلِي غَنِيٌّ (broccoli is rich).

profile.feeling: Mild onion flavour; soups and pies.

examples.tr: I cooked leek soup.
I bought fresh leeks at the market.

examples.text: يُشْبِهُ الْكُرَّاثُ الْبَصَلَ الْأَخْضَرَ، لٰكِنَّهُ أَكْبَرُ.
examples.tr: The leek looks like a spring onion, but it is bigger.

synonyms.nuance: the Egyptian form, with t (Wiktionary translation tables)

etymology.text: Borrowed from Aramaic כרתא (karrāṯā), from Akkadian karašu, from Sumerian garaš; compare Hebrew כְּרֵשָׁה (kәreshá) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew כְּרֵשָׁה and Arabic كُرَّاث share an Akkadian–Sumerian ancestor, garaš.
pitfalls: Also vocalized كَرَّاث (karrāṯ); Wiktionary lists both.
Wiktionary defines it specifically as Allium kurrat, the slender “Egyptian leek”; its translation tables use it for the European leek as well.
subtleties: Masculine mass noun: كُرَّاثٌ طَازَجٌ (fresh leek).

profile.feeling: Colourful: red, yellow, green; stuffed or in salads.

examples.tr: I like red bell peppers.
Cut the bell pepper into strips.
I bought green bell peppers.

synonyms.nuance: lit. “Rūmī (Byzantine) pepper” — the usual word in Egypt (Wiktionary)
diminutive “little pepper”, listed by Wiktionary; the everyday Levantine word

etymology.text: فِلْفِل is borrowed from Classical Persian پلپل (pilpil), from Sanskrit पिप्पलि (pippalī, “long pepper”); حُلْو means “sweet” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Egypt’s فِلْفِل رُومِيّ means “Byzantine pepper” — Rūm was the Arabic name for the (Greek-speaking) Eastern Roman Empire.
pitfalls: Masculine: فِلْفِلٌ حُلْوٌ — not *حُلْوَةٌ.
Chili differs only in the adjective: فِلْفِلٌ حَارٌّ.
subtleties: Colour adjectives follow and are diptotes: فِلْفِلٌ حُلْوٌ أَصْفَرُ (yellow pepper) — no tanwīn on the colour.

profile.feeling: Deep red, sweet and earthy; pickles and salads.

examples.tr: Beetroot juice is red in colour.
I boiled the beetroot for the salad.

examples.text: يُسْتَخْرَجُ السُّكَّرُ مِنْ نَوْعٍ مِنَ الشَّمَنْدَرِ.
examples.tr: Sugar is extracted from a kind of beet.

synonyms.nuance: the usual word in Egypt and the southern Levant; from Turkish pancar (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: Disputed (Wiktionary): either from Ottoman Turkish şamandıra (“buoy”), because of its shape, or ultimately from Sumerian šumundar (“beetroot, red plant”).

funFacts: A Turkish speaker recognises بَنْجَر at once: it is pancar.
pitfalls: Sun letter: الشَّمَنْدَرُ = aš-šamandar.
Wiktionary’s translation tables specify شَمَنْدَر أَحْمَر (red beet) for the red root; plain شَمَنْدَر is the beet in general.
subtleties: Masculine mass noun: الشَّمَنْدَرُ الْمَسْلُوقُ (boiled beetroot).

profile.feeling: Stuffed zucchini — a festive family dish across the Levant.

examples.tr: Stuffed zucchini is a famous dish.
I bought a kilo of zucchini.
Cut the zucchini and fry it in oil.

synonyms.nuance: the same word spelled with tāʾ marbūṭa — the usual spelling in Egypt

etymology.text: From an urban dialect form, a doublet of قِثَّاء (“Armenian cucumber”); Eilers derives it from Classical Persian کوسه (kōsa, “man with little or no beard”), i.e. the “hairless, smooth” fruit (Wiktionary).

funFacts: If the Persian etymology is right, zucchini is “the beardless one”.
pitfalls: Indeclinable: كُوسَا never shows case endings (like بَطَاطَا).
Feminine (Wiktionary): كُوسَا مَحْشِيَّةٌ, not *مَحْشِيٌّ.
subtleties: Zucchini, like all Cucurbita, came from the Americas; the Arabic name was transferred from Old World cucumber relatives (Wiktionary).

ref.src: Wiktionary (kaikki.org): فاصوليا, فاصولياء; the phrase has no entry

profile.feeling: Everyday home cooking: green beans with tomato and meat.

senses.def: green beans, French beans (the green pods)

examples.tr: I cooked green beans with tomatoes.
I bought fresh green beans.
Green beans are rich in fibre.

collocations.tr: green beans cooked in olive oil

synonyms.nuance: green beans in the Levant (Wiktionary gives both senses); elsewhere لُوبِيَا is the black-eyed pea
the dictionary spelling with final hamza (Wiktionary’s main entry)

etymology.text: فَاصُولِيَا (alternative form of فَاصُولِيَاء) is from Ottoman Turkish fasulye, from Greek φασούλια (fasoúlia) (Wiktionary); خَضْرَاء is the feminine of أَخْضَر, “green”.

funFacts: A Greek speaker hears φασόλια/φασούλια in فَاصُولِيَا — it came to Arabic through Turkish fasulye.
pitfalls: خَضْرَاء is a diptote: فَاصُولِيَا خَضْرَاءُ (no tanwīn), and without al- its genitive ends in -a (خَضْرَاءَ).
Plain فَاصُولِيَا can also mean dried beans; add خَضْرَاء for the green pods.
subtleties: فَاصُولِيَا itself is indeclinable (ends in -ā); the case shows only on خَضْرَاء, which is feminine because فَاصُولِيَا is.

ref.src: Wiktionary (kaikki.org): بصل; the phrase has no entry

profile.feeling: Fresh and sharp; with ful, salads and grilled meat.

examples.tr: Chop the spring onions finely.
I add spring onions to the salad.
I bought a bunch of spring onions.

profile.synonymsNone: No common single-word synonym in MSA.

etymology.text: بَصَل “onion” (a common Semitic word, Wiktionary) + أَخْضَر “green”.
etymology.src: Wiktionary (kaikki.org): بصل; the phrase has no entry

funFacts: The Arabic image is the same as American English “green onion”.
pitfalls: أَخْضَر is a diptote: بَصَلٌ أَخْضَرُ (no tanwīn on the adjective), بَصَلٍ أَخْضَرَ in the genitive.
subtleties: Collective and masculine: الْبَصَلُ الْأَخْضَرُ طَازَجٌ (the spring onions are fresh).

profile.feeling: Aromatic; soups and stews.

senses.def: celery (mass noun; a stick = عُودُ كَرَفْسٍ)

examples.tr: Add the celery to the soup.
I bought a stick of celery.
Celery has a strong smell.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym in Modern Standard Arabic.

etymology.text: Borrowed from Middle Persian karafs (“celery”), from Classical Syriac kərap̄sā (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Turkish kereviz (celery) comes from the same Persian word.
pitfalls: Vowels: ka-rafs (كَرَفْس) with sukūn on f. Unvocalized كرفس can also be read كُرْفُس, a rare word for cotton (Wiktionary).
subtleties: Masculine mass noun: كَرَفْسٌ طَازَجٌ (fresh celery).

profile.feeling: Summer evenings: grilled corn sold on the corniche.

senses.def: maize, corn (collective; Wiktionary uses the same form for one grain)

examples.tr: We eat grilled corn on the beach.
Corn oil is light.
Corn is planted in summer.

examples.text: يُصْنَعُ الْخُبْزُ فِي السُّودَانِ مِنَ الذُّرَةِ الرَّفِيعَةِ.
examples.tr: In Sudan bread is made from sorghum.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym in Modern Standard Arabic.

etymology.text: Perhaps from the root ذ ر و / ذ ر ي (“to scatter”) — Wiktionary marks this as uncertain.

funFacts: English durra (sorghum) is this Arabic word.
pitfalls: ذُرَة (ḏura, corn: short u, no šadda) and ذَرَّة (ḏarra, atom, speck: with šadda) are both written ذرة without vowels.
Sun letter: الذُّرَةُ = aḏ-ḏura.
subtleties: Feminine (it ends in ة): الذُّرَةُ الْمَشْوِيَّةُ (grilled corn).
